entries.narration:
Our engine starts as an empty folder called miniflow, and two tools turn it into a project.

The first is Node. In the terminal we ask for its version, and it answers twenty-six point thirteen. The side pane shows what that one command carries. Inside Node is V8, the engine that runs JavaScript, the same one that runs it in Chrome. Around V8 is Node's standard library: files, paths, networking, everything a browser never lets a page touch. When our engine writes a picture to disk, that is the standard library at work.

The second tool is npm, and it ships with Node: the terminal shows its version, eleven point twenty. Its job is the package. We run npm init with the yes flag, which accepts every default, and one more setting that asks for modules. npm would print the whole file it wrote. We send that echo nowhere, because the editor shows the same package dot json. Most of it is a name, a version and an empty test script. The highlighted line is the one that matters to us: type is module. It means every file here uses import and export, the standard JavaScript module syntax, rather than Node's older require.

Down the side pane, npm points the other way, at the registry. That is where the packages we install will come from, starting with TypeScript itself a few sections from now. For the moment, the folder has a package file and nothing else.

Next, we give it a file that draws something.

The first file is main dot ts, and on the right of the explorer it is marked new, along with the picture it writes.

The editor shows its heart. A type called Box describes a box with a title, a width and a height. The box itself is a checkout box, eighty wide and twenty tall, and a padding of twelve goes around it. The three highlighted lines carry types: the shape of a box, the box that must match it, and a padding that must be a number. Below them, the file builds a little SVG string, one rectangle and one line of text, and writes it to a folder called out.

We run it with plain node. No compiler, no build step. Node twenty-six reads a dot ts file directly. The side pane shows how. Node does not check the types at all. It strips them, replacing every annotation with blank space so the line numbers stay put, and hands V8 the JavaScript that is left. V8 runs it, and Node's file system module writes the picture.

The bottom panel is that picture, out slash box dot svg, opened in a browser. One rounded box, one word: checkout. It is a hundred and four by forty-four, the eighty of content plus twelve on each side.

That is the whole engine for now: a type, a value, and a file. But we said Node strips the types without reading them. So where do they actually go?

This is a detour, to see what happens to a type once it is written.

On the left is the picture of one file and two jobs. The same main dot ts feeds two very different programs. One is tsc, the TypeScript compiler, whose job is to check: it reads every type and either reports errors or stays silent. The other job is erasing. Node does it every time we run the file, and tsc can do it too, writing the JavaScript out as a file. Either way the result is plain JavaScript, and V8 runs that, knowing nothing about types at all.

To see the erasing on screen, we ask tsc to write its output into a folder called emit. The terminal shows the command, and tsc prints nothing, which for tsc means success.

Now compare the two files. On top is the source, with the type of a box and the annotated values highlighted. Underneath is what tsc wrote. The Box type is simply gone, the colon and its type after the box have vanished, and so has the number after the padding. Every line that remains is the same JavaScript as before, with a semicolon added at each end. No checks are left behind, and nothing in the running program remembers that a box was supposed to have a numeric width.

That is the deal TypeScript makes. Types cost nothing at run time, because they are not there at run time. So the only time anything checks them is before the program runs. Next, we install the checker.

Node runs our file, but nothing has checked it yet. That is tsc's job, so we install it.

In the terminal, npm installs two packages as development dependencies: TypeScript, pinned to seven point oh point two, and the type definitions for Node itself, which tell the checker what Node's file system module looks like. npm reports four packages added in a fraction of a second, and the explorer gains a lock file and the node modules folder, greyed out because we never edit it.

tsc needs to know how to check, and that is the tsconfig dot json in the editor. It targets the newest JavaScript, uses Node's own module rules, and loads Node's types. Two options are highlighted. Strict switches on the full set of checks, the ones every serious TypeScript project uses. And no emit says: check only. Node already runs the file, so tsc should never write JavaScript next to it.

The side pane follows one run. tsc reads the config, then checks main dot ts and every file it imports, and ends in one of two places: a list of errors and an exit code of one, or silence and an exit code of zero.

We ask for the version, seven point oh point two, and then run the check. The last line of the terminal is the answer: nothing at all. Silence is tsc's way of saying the program is sound.

So now we have two tools reading one file. Next, we make them disagree.

Here is one small mistake, the kind a real program makes every day. In the highlighted line, the box's width is written in quotes, so it is a string rather than a number.

First, the checker. tsc stops at line five, column thirty-nine, exactly where the width is, with error TS2322: type string is not assignable to type number. The Box type said width is a number, and tsc held the value to it.

Now the same file, run with node. It does not complain at all. It strips the types, as we saw, and runs what is left. And the result is wrong in a way that is very JavaScript. The second highlighted line adds the padding to the width. With a number, eighty plus twenty-four is a hundred and four. With a string, the plus sign joins text instead, so the width becomes eight thousand and twenty-four. Node writes a box more than eight thousand pixels wide, and prints that size as if nothing had happened.

The side pane draws the two paths out of one file. The checked path refuses it. The run path draws it anyway. Underneath is the table to remember. A wrong type is refused by tsc and run by Node. A syntax error, a missing brace, is refused by both.

That is why the check is a separate step, and why it has to run before the program does. Node will not save us from a wrong type. But there is one kind of TypeScript that Node does refuse, and it is the next section.

Our box is about to get a colour, and many TypeScript tutorials would reach for an enum to name the colours. The editor shows one: an enum called Tone, with two members, source and store, and the box now carries a tone.

We run the file with node, and this time Node refuses. We asked it to leave out its own internal stack frames so the whole error fits, and what is left is the part that matters. It points at line three, underlines the enum, and names the problem: error unsupported TypeScript syntax. A TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode.

The side pane explains strip-only mode. Node's whole job here is deleting: it removes types and writes nothing new. On the left is everything it can delete. A type alias, a colon and a type, a cast with as: remove the characters, and valid JavaScript remains.

On the right is syntax it refuses, because it means something at run time. An enum becomes a real object, with a property for each member, so somebody has to write new JavaScript for it. The same is true of a namespace, and of a constructor parameter that declares a private field, which turns into an assignment. tsc knows how to emit that JavaScript. Node, which only erases, refuses.

So we have a rule worth keeping: write only TypeScript that can be erased. But right now, only Node enforces it, and only when the file runs. Next, we teach the checker the same rule.

The rule is simple: only syntax Node can delete. The question is who enforces it, and when.

The editor shows the answer, one new option in tsconfig, highlighted: erasable syntax only, set to true. It tells the checker to treat anything Node would refuse as an error.

The terminal runs the check again, on the same file with the same enum. tsc now stops at line three, column six, the word Tone, with error TS1294: this syntax is not allowed when erasable syntax only is enabled.

The side pane shows why that matters. One rule, two enforcers. Node enforces it when the file runs, and only then. tsc now enforces it while we write, in the editor and in the check, long before anything runs. The note says it plainly: the checker now refuses, up front, what Node would refuse only later.

This flag also explains a choice we will keep for the rest of the film. You will not see an enum here, or a namespace, or a constructor that declares its own fields. When we need named colours, in the next course, we will build them from a union of plain string values, which is erasable and, as it turns out, more precise.

That closes the first file. We have a package, a main file that draws one box, a checker with strict settings, and a rule that keeps the two tools in agreement. Next, we describe a whole scene in types.

Our engine is going to draw diagrams, and a diagram starts with a box. So the first thing to describe is one box, as plain values.

The editor holds five of them: an id, a title, a width, a padding, and whether the box is visible. Notice that none of them has a type written next to it. TypeScript does not need one. When a value is right there, the checker infers its type from it, and the side pane shows what it decides.

The interesting part is the difference between const and let. A const can never change, so TypeScript keeps the exact value as the type. The id is not just any string: its type is the single word orders. The width is exactly ninety-six. Visible is exactly true. Padding is declared with let, because it changes on the next line, so TypeScript widens it to number: any number may follow.

Those are the three primitive types we will use everywhere: string, number and boolean. Every other type in this film is built out of them.

The terminal runs the two steps we will use from now on. First the check, which is silent, so everything holds. Then the run. The first line prints the five values, with the padding now sixteen. The second line asks JavaScript itself what kind each value is, and it answers string, number, number and boolean. That is the run-time view, which is much coarser than the checker's.

That exactness is about to pay off. Next, we give the box a colour, chosen from a fixed set.

Every box in our diagrams has a tone, a colour family that says what the box is: a source of data, a store, a service. There are exactly seven, and anything else is a mistake.

The highlighted type at the top says so. Tone is a union of seven string literals, joined by vertical bars, and the bar reads as or. The side pane draws what that means: a type is a set of values, and this set has exactly seven members. Neutral, source, ingest, store, serve, consume and infra. Nothing else belongs.

So when the item declares its tone as a Tone and sets it to store, the checker agrees. And when a scratch file, try dot ts, makes the typo we all make, stroe, the terminal shows the result: error TS2820, type stroe is not assignable to type Tone. And then the checker adds a suggestion of its own: did you mean store? It can, because it knows the whole set.

Compare that with the last highlighted line. A variable called kind is declared with let and the word item. Because it may change, TypeScript widens it to string, the set of every text there is, and so the next line can set it to anything at all without a complaint. A wide type checks almost nothing.

The run prints the item with its tone in brackets: store, orders, Orders DB.

Seven allowed words is the first real rule our engine has. Next, we gather an item's fields into one shape.

Loose variables do not make a diagram. We need one value per box, with all its fields together, and a type that says what those fields are.

That type now lives in its own file, model dot ts, in a new source folder. The editor shows it. Tone has moved here, and under it is an interface called Item. An interface names a shape: an id that is a string, a title that is a string, and two fields with a question mark, sub and tone. The question mark means optional, and the side pane's table marks the difference: id and title must be there, sub and tone may be left out.

You could write the same shape with the type keyword and an equals sign instead. For an object, the two are nearly interchangeable. We will use interface for object shapes and type for everything else, which is the common habit.

The main file imports that type and builds the orders item, and the checker holds it to the shape. It has an id, a title and a tone, so it fits. The scratch file tries an item with a misspelled field, titel, and the terminal shows what happens: error TS2561. An object literal may only specify known properties, and titel does not exist in Item. Did you mean title? Mistyped field names are among the commonest bugs in JavaScript, and here one is caught before anything runs.

The run prints the same line as before, now read from one object. Next, we look closely at that question mark.

An optional field is a promise that the value might not be there. TypeScript takes that promise seriously, and so must we.

The side pane shows what the question mark really means. The type of an item's sub is not string. It is string or undefined, and every use of it has two branches. The orders item has a sub, one row per order. The API item has none at all.

The scratch file ignores that and asks for the length of the API's sub directly. The terminal shows the checker's answer: error TS18048, api dot sub is possibly undefined. In plain JavaScript that line would crash at run time with a type error. Here it never gets the chance.

The editor shows the two operators that handle the missing case, highlighted. The double question mark supplies a default: if the tone is undefined, use neutral. Then a plain condition builds the sub text only when there is one. And the question mark followed by a dot, optional chaining, stops early: if the sub is undefined, the whole expression is undefined instead of an error.

The run walks both items. The orders item has no tone, so it prints neutral, with its sub and a length of seventeen. The API prints serve, no sub, and a length of undefined, without a crash.

One item is not a diagram, though. Next, we put items inside a group.

A diagram has structure: boxes sit inside groups, and the groups sit side by side or stacked. That structure is a tree, and the next shape in our model describes it.

The editor adds an interface called Group, highlighted at the bottom of the model file. A group has an id and a title, a direction that is a literal union of row or column, and children. The children field is typed as Item followed by square brackets, an array of items. Every element must be an Item, and the checker will hold each one to that shape.

The side pane draws the value from the main file. The data group lays out its children in a column, and the column holds two items: orders and email. One parent, an array of children. That is a tree, even if for now it is only one level deep.

The main file prints the group's title and direction, then loops over its children with for of, and prints each one indented beneath it, with neutral as the default tone. The run shows the result: Data, in a column, then store orders and consume email, one step in.

The scratch file is gone, because nothing here is meant to fail. But look at the limit we just built in. A group can hold items, and only items. In a real diagram a group holds other groups too: a data center holds racks, and racks hold servers. Next, we let a child be either kind, and that needs a union of shapes.

A child in our tree can now be an item or a group. TypeScript can describe that, and the trick is a single field.

The model file gives each shape a type field with a literal value. Every Item has type item, and every Group has type group. Then the highlighted line names the combination: a SceneNode is an Item or a Group. And a group's children are now SceneNodes, so groups can hold groups, as deep as we like.

That type field is called the discriminant, and the side pane shows why it matters. A SceneNode on its own could be either shape, so the checker lets us read only the fields both share. But the moment we test the tag, the union splits in two. If type is item, it is an Item, with a title, a sub and a tone. If type is group, it is a Group, with a direction and children.

With that, the whole checkout scene can be written as data. It is in its own file in a new scenes folder: a browser, an API, a services group holding payments, inventory and a queue, and a data group holding the orders database and email. The tsconfig gains one setting, allow importing TypeScript extensions, because the main file now imports a value from a dot ts file.

The main file tests each top-level node's tag, and the run prints them: the browser and the API as items, then services with three children and data with two.

The test on the tag is called narrowing, and it is the next section.

The printer now turns the whole checkout scene into an outline, and it does that with narrowing: following the type through each branch of the code.

The function in the editor takes a node and a depth. The highlighted switch looks at the node's type field, and the side pane follows what the checker knows at each point. Before the switch, the node is an Item or a Group. Inside the item case, it is an Item, so the code may read its sub and its tone. Inside the group case, it is a Group, so it may read its children, and the function calls itself for each child, one level deeper. That is recursion, and it is how a function walks a tree whose depth it does not know.

Narrowing is not limited to switch. Inside the item case, a check that the sub is not undefined narrows it from string or undefined to string. A test with typeof, or with the in operator, which asks whether an object has a field, narrows the same way. The checker reads ordinary JavaScript conditions and updates the type to match.

The run shows the scene as an outline. Checkout on top, then the browser and the API with their subs, then the services group, in a column, with payments, inventory and the queue indented under it, and the data group with the orders database and email.

The printer handles every kind of node there is. Next, we add a third kind, and see whether the checker notices.

Our scenes need one more kind of node: a note, a short line of text that explains the diagram. Adding it shows one of TypeScript's most useful habits.

The model gains a Note interface, with type note and some text, and the SceneNode union grows to three members. The checkout scene opens with a note. But the printer's switch still handles only items and groups.

The highlighted default branch is what catches that. It assigns the node to a variable whose type is never. Never is the empty set: a type with no values at all. The side pane's table follows what the node can still be as the switch goes down. Before notes, after the item case only Group was left, and after the group case nothing was: never. So the assignment was fine.

With notes added, there is a leftover. After both cases, the node can still be a Note, and a Note cannot be assigned to never. The terminal shows the checker pointing at exactly that line, with error TS2322: type Note is not assignable to type never.

This is the payoff of a discriminated union. Whenever the model gains a new kind of node, every switch that forgot it becomes a compile error, at the line that needs the new case. Nothing slips through to run time unhandled. In a codebase with many such switches, that is the difference between a quick change and a hunt.

One more case for the note, and the outline prints it. Next course, we work out where each box goes.

Before the engine can draw a box, it has to know how big the box is. That is a job for a function, and functions are where TypeScript's types do some of their best work.

The new file, measure dot ts, holds two. The first is measure. Its parameters say what it takes: an item, and a padding with a default of twelve, so a caller may leave it out. After the parentheses, the return type says what it gives back: a Size, an object with a width and a height. Inside, it takes the item's title and sub, finds the longest line, and multiplies its length by nine point six, the width of one character in our monospace measure. Twenty pixels per line gives the height, and the padding goes on every side.

The side pane writes the whole function as one type: it takes an Item and an optional number, and returns a Size. That type is a value's type like any other, and later we will pass functions around by it.

The second function is row. Its last parameter starts with three dots, which makes it a rest parameter: any number of sizes, collected into an array. It adds up the widths, keeps the tallest height, and adds a gap between each pair.

The run measures each top-level item. The browser is a hundred and forty-nine by sixty-four. The two items in a row, with a gap of twenty-four, come to three hundred and thirty-two. And the email box with no padding at all is forty-eight by twenty: just its text.

Items are easy. Next, a group, whose size depends on everything inside it.

A group's size is not written anywhere. It is the sizes of its children, arranged in a row or a column, plus the group's own padding and title. And a child might be a group too. The natural way to compute that is a function that calls itself.

The new layout file has one function for every kind of node, called size of. The switch from Course 3 is back: an item measures its title and sub, a note measures its text. The highlighted group case is the interesting one. It loops over the children and calls size of on each, then combines them: in a row, widths add up and the tallest height wins, and in a column it is the other way round. Then it adds the gaps between children, room for the title, and padding on each side.

The side pane shows what happens when it runs on the services group. The call for services makes three more calls, one per child, and each child is an item, which returns straight away. That is the base case, the case that stops the recursion. Only when all three have answered can the group add them up. The call tree has exactly the shape of the scene tree, which is why recursion fits trees so well.

The run prints every top-level node. The note is two hundred and sixty-four by forty-four. The services group, three items stacked with two gaps, a title and padding, is a hundred and seventy-three by two hundred and ninety-six.

We have sizes. Next, we give every box a position, and keep them all in a map.

A size says how big a box is. To draw it, we also need where it is: an x and a y. Together they make a Rect, and the layout will produce one for every node.

The layout file gains a function called place. It works top-down: it records a node's rect, and if the node is a group, it walks across or down its children, handing each one its position. The results go into a Map, from a node's id to its rect. The side pane draws it: a key on the left, a rect on the right, ten keys in all, one per node.

A map has one property that matters a great deal. Asking for a key that is not there does not crash. It returns undefined. So TypeScript types the result of get as Rect or undefined. The main file deals with that honestly. It asks for the orders rect, and an if narrows it to a Rect before using it. The run prints orders at eight hundred and fifty-three, forty-four.

The scratch file takes a shortcut. After get, it adds an exclamation mark, the non-null assertion, which tells the checker: trust me, this is never undefined. The checker trusts it. But there is no node called cart. The terminal shows the result: a type error at run time, cannot read properties of undefined, reading x.

The exclamation mark does not check anything. It only silences the checker, so the crash moves to run time. Use it only when you can prove the value is there.

Next, a cleaner way to combine children: a function that takes a function.

The group case of size of had a loop with two running totals and an if inside. It works, but it says how rather than what. Higher-order functions, functions that take other functions, let us say what.

The editor shows two small arrow functions, row and column. Each takes two sizes and returns one: row puts them side by side with a gap, column stacks them. The highlighted line is the whole group case now. Map turns every child into its size. Then reduce folds that list down to a single size, using row or column depending on the group's direction. And the function we hand to reduce is just a value, chosen by a condition one line earlier.

The side pane follows the fold for the services group. Its three children are a hundred and forty-nine by sixty-four, the same again, and a hundred and forty by sixty-four. Reduce combines the first two with column, then combines the result with the third. What comes out is the widest width and the heights added with two gaps: a hundred and forty-nine by two hundred and forty. The padding and title then go around it, exactly as before.

TypeScript checks the plumbing. Reduce expects a function that takes two sizes and returns a size, and both row and column have that type, so either may be passed.

The run prints the whole layout with console dot table: every node, with its x, y, width and height. Services sits at six hundred and forty-four, and its children start twelve pixels in.

Next, a function that works for any type at all.

We keep needing the same walk: visit every node in the tree, ask each one a question, and collect the answers. The question changes, but the walk does not. A generic function lets us write the walk once.

The new file, tree dot ts, has a function called map tree. The angle brackets after its name introduce a type parameter, T. It stands for whatever type the question returns. The parameter f is a function from a node to a T, and map tree returns an array of T. Inside, it asks the node, then recurses into any children with flat map, so the answers come back as one flat list.

The side pane shows the payoff. In the main file, the first call asks each node for its id. The id is a string, so for that call TypeScript fills in T as string, and the result is an array of strings. The second call asks for each node's width, so T becomes number, and the result is an array of numbers. Nobody wrote string or number at the call. The checker inferred T from the function passed in.

That matters on the next line. Math dot max needs numbers, and because the widths are typed as an array of numbers, it is allowed. If the walk had returned something loose, that line could not be checked.

The run prints the ten ids, the ten widths, and the widest, two hundred and sixty-four, which is the note.

A type parameter can be anything. Sometimes we need it to be anything with a particular shape. That is next.

A scene's ids must be unique, or the layout's map would quietly overwrite one rect with another. A function that indexes things by id can check that, and it should work for nodes, rects, or anything else, as long as it has an id.

That is what the highlighted line says. Index by id takes a type parameter N, but the word extends puts a bound on it: N must have an id that is a string. Inside the function, that bound is what allows reading node dot id at all. Without it, N could be a number, and the checker would refuse.

The side pane's table lists what may be passed. An array of scene nodes is fine, because every node has an id. So is a list of plain objects with an id and a width, which have nothing to do with our model. The scratch file passes objects with a name instead, and the terminal shows the checker's refusal: error TS2353, name does not exist in a type with only an id.

The constraint has a second effect, just as useful. N is still the full type of what was passed in. So when the map of sizes is read back, the entry for queue is known to have a width, a number, not just an id. The run prints a hundred and twenty for it, and ten nodes indexed from the scene, with the browser's type read straight back as item.

A bound like that is how library code stays general without giving up its types.

Next, a walk that stops halfway through.

Map tree visits every node, whether we need them all or not. Sometimes we want to stop early: find the first title too wide for its column and report it. A generator walks the tree one node at a time, and only as far as asked.

The function in the editor has an asterisk after the word function. That makes it a generator. Instead of returning a list, it yields one node and pauses. Yield star hands over to a nested walk, so the children come out in order. Its return type says what comes out: a Generator of scene nodes.

The main file loops over it with for of. Each turn of the loop asks the generator for the next node, and the generator resumes exactly where it paused. The loop checks each item's title against a limit of eight characters, and breaks at the first one longer.

The side pane counts what happened. The loop visited the note, the browser, the API, the services group, payments, and then inventory, whose title is nine characters, and the run prints too wide: Inventory. Six visited. The four greyed-out nodes at the bottom, the queue, the data group, orders and email, were never reached. Breaking out of the loop stopped the generator, so no work was done for them.

That laziness is the point. A generator does no work until it is asked, and stops when nobody asks. On a scene of ten nodes it hardly matters. On a diagram of thousands, it is the difference between scanning all of them and scanning six.

Next, protecting a rect from being changed by accident.

Once the layout has placed a box, nothing else should move it by accident. In JavaScript, objects are shared, which makes that kind of accident easy. TypeScript can rule it out.

The side pane shows the trap. The scratch file loops over the map's rects, and the loop variable r is a second name for an object the map already holds. Two names, one object. So when the loop shifts every r forty pixels to the right, it is changing the layout's own rects in place, for everyone who reads them later. Nothing about that line looks dangerous.

The editor shows the defence, highlighted: the fields of Rect, and of Size, are now marked readonly. The objects are the same at run time, but the checker refuses any assignment to them. The terminal shows it catching the scratch file: error TS2540, cannot assign to x, because it is a read-only property.

So how does anything change a picture's position? By making a new value. The new fit file does that. Fit takes the content's size and a frame's size, keeps a margin of four percent on each side, and works out one scale and an offset that centres the content. The scale is clamped between a twentieth and four. It returns a fresh Transform and never touches a rect.

The run measures the content, a thousand and fifty-three by two hundred and ninety-six, and fits it into a frame of twelve eighty by seven twenty. The scale comes out at about one point one two, with the picture centred.

Next, a detour, to watch the whole layout happen.

This is a detour, to watch a whole layout happen, pass by pass, on a scene with a problem in it.

The scene is self, miniflow's picture of itself: a model, an engine group holding layout and route, and a draw step. One title, highlighted in the scene file, is a deliberate fault. It is sixty characters long, far wider than its neighbours.

The left side names the three passes. Measure goes bottom-up, because a parent cannot know its size until its children do. Place goes top-down, because a child cannot know its position until its parent has one. Fit comes last, and works on the finished picture.

For this lab, the layout logs every step, and the terminal shows the real order. Measure runs first: model, then the long layout item, then route, and only then engine, after both its children. The layout item measures six hundred by forty-four, so the engine group, which must hold it, grows to six hundred and twenty-four wide. Then place runs from the top: model at zero, engine next to it, its two children inside, and draw pushed all the way over to eight hundred and twenty-one, because the column in front of it grew.

That is the rule on the left: a title wider than its column grows the column, and everything after it moves over. Nothing is ever clipped, because clipping would hide words the author wrote. A diagram that grows too wide is fixed by the author, never silently by the engine.

Finally, fit scales the whole nine hundred and fifty-one by one eighty-eight picture into the frame at about one point two four. Next course, we draw it.
